entry.title: The 2026 S.-T. Yau Contest
entry.content:
The S.-T. Yau College Student Mathematics Contest is an undergraduate competition founded by Shing-Tung Yau in 2010. I took the Algebra and Number Theory exam. The format was five problems in two hours, modeled closely after graduate entrance exams. I ended up getting 39th place, which is an honorable mention, and a result I'm very happy with.

A Problem From 2025

To give an idea of what the exam is like, here is Problem 5 from the 2025 Algebra and Number Theory paper.

Let $f(X)=X^5-X+1$, let $E$ be its splitting field over $\mathbb Q$, and set $D=\operatorname{Disc}(f)$. Recall that $\operatorname{Disc}(X^5+aX+b)=4^4a^5+5^5b^4$.

  1. Show that $f$ is irreducible.
  2. Determine all finite primes ramified in $E$ and compute the orders of their inertia subgroups.
  3. Show that $E/\mathbb Q(\sqrt D)$ is unramified at every finite prime and ramified at the Archimedean primes.
  4. Show that $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$ is generated by its inertia subgroups.
  5. Show that $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)\cong S_5$ and $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q(\sqrt D))\cong A_5$.

Here is an extremely abbreviated solution. The reduction of $f$ modulo $5$ is irreducible by Artin-Shreier theory, while $D=5^5-4^4=2869=19\cdot151$ is square-free. Therefore the only ramified primes are $19$ and $151$, and their inertia groups have order two and act as transpositions. The group generated by all finite inertia groups is normal, and its fixed field is unramified over $\mathbb Q$ at every finite prime; Minkowski therefore says that the fixed field is $\mathbb Q$. Consequently the Galois group is a transitive subgroup of $S_5$ generated by transpositions, hence is $S_5$. The square root of the discriminant transforms by the sign character, giving the $A_5$ claim and finite unramifiedness over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt D)$. Finally, $f$ has only one real root, so $E$ is totally imaginary whereas $\mathbb Q(\sqrt D)$ is real; its Archimedean primes ramify.

The 2026 Exam

Here is the full 2026 Algebra and Number Theory exam.

My favorite problem was Problem 3. Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathcal O_{\overline K}$ the ring of all algebraic integers in an algebraic closure. The problem asks you to prove that $a,b\in\mathcal O_K$ are coprime if and only if there is some $u\in\mathcal O_{\overline K}$ for which $au+b$ is a unit.

Here is a solution sketch. Suppose $(a,b)=1$; the trivial cases aside, choose $n$ such that $(-b)^n\equiv1\pmod a$, which is possible because $(\mathcal O_K/(a))^\times$ is finite. Since the degree-$(n-1)$ monomials in $a$ and $-b$ generate $(a,b)^{n-1}=(1)$, we can choose $c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1}\in\mathcal O_K$ so that

$$ (-b)^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_j a^{n-j}(-b)^j=1. $$

Set $P(T)=T^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jT^j$ and take any root $u$ of $P$. Then $u$ is integral, while $a^nP((Y-b)/a)$ is a monic integral polynomial with constant term $1$ having $au+b$ as a root, so $au+b$ is a unit. Conversely, if a prime ideal contained both $a$ and $b$, any prime above it in a finite extension containing $u$ and $(au+b)^{-1}$ would contain the unit $au+b$, a contradiction.

I liked this problem because even if you know all the machinery, it is still quite hard to come up with this solution. It was a very rewarding experience to solve this one.

The Experience

After solving problems 3 and 4, there was barely any time left. This was despite the fact that neither took extremely long to think through, especially problem 4, which was a mechanical application of Dedekind's criterion. Writing the solutions consumed almost the entire exam. I suspect my writeups were much more verbose then they needed to be, I will try to correct this next year.

I searched for partials in many of the other problems, though without having a score breakdown, I'm not sure how successful I was. I was particularly sad about problem 5: I had not read far enough into Neukirch to know the relevant local-field material, but only barely, I had stopped just before the useful part. In the end, I ran out of time failing to get a Hermite normal form solution working for problem 1.

I also made the mistake of not attempting problem 2 because its statement looked long and I was in a time crunch. It turned out to be by far the freest problem on the exam, and solving it would have gotten me to finals.

Still, I am hopeful that I can make finals next year. Congratulations to Jack for making it this time! We solved almost disjoint sets of problems, so together we would have made one excellent contestant. Unfortunately, the individual contest remains individual.

My Opinion

Overall, the exam is very fun and rewarding. It is fun to test one's mettle against what is essentially a souped up graduate qualifying exam. It's also rare that one gets to use advanced machinery in a competition format.

The exam itself is very different from the other math competitions I've done. With exceptions, it is sometimes a knowledge check, and a lot of questions can be boiled down to:

Do you know this machinery, and how fast can you write it up?

Due to the insane time constraints, it's mandatory to have seen a good amount of the problems (many of which are standard textbook exercises) almost verbatim. Problem 4 is a good example, I got lucky to have studied Dedekind's criterion, otherwise it would have taken way longer. It is therefore very important how well the exam overlaps with your knowledge, and how fast of a writer you are (this might be the reason the winners are very variable each year, without many repeat successes). This is not a bad thing though, knowing machinery is extremely important, and it feels good to read a problem and instantly say "I know how to do this, I read about it in X textbook".

My only complaint is the distribution of problems. Despite allegedly being about algebra and number theory, this year's exam was 5/5 problems on number theory. From what I can tell, there is no consistent standard for what the format looks like from year to year. In my preparations for the Topology and Geometry Exam, I "strategically" sacrificed Riemannian geometry. After all, it's only one out of the thirteen categories on the syllabus. I still remember the sheer hopelessness I felt upon being greeted by 5/6 problems requiring a very strong base in Riemannian geometry to solve, 3 of those being purely Riemannian geometry. I'll try not to make the same mistake next year.

entry.title: Writing LaTeX
entry.content:
These are my thoughts and opinions on writing LaTeX code. Of course, this is just my way of doing things, I do not claim that this is the best way of doing things.

The Setup

In general, my philosophy for setting up and writing LaTeX prioritizes the following three things in decreasing order of importance:

  1. Convenience, ease of use, and laziness
  2. Aesthetic quality of the result
  3. Cleanliness and organization of the code

After a long time, I have decided that the best way to accomplish this is with the following structure:

Preamble
documentclass:
PSet
Paper
Report

I believe this is the standard way to do things, but nonetheless, I have met a surprising number of people who are unfamiliar with this methodology. Essentially, I put stuff in my preamble that I want to include in all my tex files. This includes things like math commands, some packages, and the way I like the enumerate environment to act.

In each .cls file I import the preamble via the \input{} command. I have different document classes defined for different purposes. The document class contains all the specific stuff, like theorem environments, code for how the title and bibliography should look, etc. Then, using the document class is as simple as putting it in the \documentclass{} command.

This avoids having long and identical preambles at the start of everything I write, and means that any change will propagate through everything I do later.

In terms of the actual aesthetics, my taste is generally quite conservative for subjects like physics and math, and less so for things such as chemistry or biology. Perhaps this is because in mathematics, one needs to devote all their brainpower to reasoning through the mathematics, so clutter on the page is just distracting. On the other hand, biology and chemistry can be quite nonlinear, and can get so confusing and complicated that having colors or boxes as visual guides is often necessary in order to not get lost. This is all just speculation though.

The Writing

One of the most important personal choices in how you write latex code is the code editor. I would conjecture the most popular options are:

  1. Overleaf
  2. Visual Studio Code
  3. Vim or Neovim
  4. Texmaker or some other dedicated software

I would claim that Visual Studio Code or Neovim are the best options. They both have the advantage of customizability, a vibrant plugin system, offline use, and highly optimized shortcuts. More broadly, they are capable and customizable code editors. People have spent years and countless hours perfecting the process of writing code, and writing LaTeX is quite similar to writing code, so it makes sense to use a code editor. I also write a lot of code, so it makes sense to use the same software for both tasks.

I personally use Neovim, which I learned around freshman year and after a period of getting used to it I find it gives a nice coding experience. I am by no means a neovim wizard, however I know all the basic keybinds needed to get the job done. I would conjecture that it makes writing text feel a bit smoother and more subconscious. For instance, physics has a lot of integrals which are a pain to write out like \int_{-\infty}^\infty f \, dx. However due to LuaSnip, if I type intinf ENTER f TAB x then I'm done since I have a shortcut for these integrals. There is a much more direct line from by brain to the text than if I didn't have these shortcuts (it is worth noting VSCode has equivalent functionality to this). These days I use LazyVim, which is quite customizable but at the same time gives a very nice premade setup and reduces maintenance load.

entry.title: Math Competitions
entry.content:
I tentatively believe that I have managed to give a very good performance in the Putnam exam. Of course, I still need to wait for scores to come out, but after looking at AOPS solutions and comparing to mine I'm confident that I did extremely well.

Mindset

Math competitions have probably been my biggest hobby since high school (about seven years running). Broadly, I would conjecture that math competitions test the following things in decreasing order of importance:

  1. Your problem solving abilities and intuition, especially as it pertains to the topics covered by the exam (elem nmbr theory, combo, etc)
  2. Your ability to handle extreme pressure
  3. Your luck, how well the problems are suited to your skills
  4. Your speed

Due to studying so much over a long period of time, and my mock test performances, I would claim that I am in decent standing in terms of (1), at least in the subjects that I focus on. However (2) is a big issue for me. When you are studying hours a day for a competition that shows up only once a year, and you've historically had disappointing performances, that kind of pressure can annihilate your sleep the night before and make you unable to even read the problem statements correctly.

In terms of getting over anxiety on math competitions, a good way might be to fully dissociate yourself from the result of the competition. This is of course easier said than done, but I would say I have achieved this on the most recent contest. Another important factor was the testing room. UChicago as a whole does not care much about math competitions. We've previously been packed into a tiny lecture hall, with those crappy desks with a fold out contraption that can't even fit a single piece of paper (If you're in college, I know you know what I'm talking about). I was bumping elbows with the people next to me since every single seat was filled. If you ask me, this is extremely disrespectful to hundreds or thousands of hours students put into this exam. We only ask to be accommodated a single day out of the entire year.

After a lot of emailing and pushing towards the administration, we managed to get a whopping two rooms this year. Unfortunately, we still had the fold out contraptions instead of a real desk, however, there at least were two feet of space between me and the next student and a place to put my pens and scratch paper other than the floor.

I will say that on this most recent competition, I felt calm, focused, and relaxed. I even managed to sleep the night before the exam. This definitely boosted my performance. Even besides these factors, the test also felt perfectly suited for my skillset (factor (3)). The analysis problems (my worst subject) were all early in the exam, and the "deciding problems" in the 3-5 range were quite algebraic. My favorite categories in the MIT sheets are linear algebra, algebra, and congruences, so you might guess that this past exam would suit me.

Preparations

In order to prepare for the 2024 competition, I did nearly all the exam problems from the past 15ish years. The downside to this is that going into 2025 I had "run out" of problems to do since the earlier years are not very representative of the modern exam. Therefore, I needed a new source of problems to do.

I figured that the MIT students are always dominating the Putnam, and a quick google search pulls up many claims that Yufei Zhao has perfected the art of training Putnam competitors (a claim I wholeheartedly believe). Therefore, I started doing the problem sheets from their Putnam seminar. I must deeply thank Professor Zhao for putting these problems online.

Over a very long period of time I managed to finish a large amount of the problems. In terms of how I did these problems, this was my procedure:

  1. Select a category based on my mood and vibes.
  2. Try to solve a problem; if I can't I'll come back to it later or collaborate with someone else (usually my friend Jack).
  3. If I do solve the problem, I'll write up a solution sketch to make sure I'm not fooling myself.
  4. After solving, I'll try to find other solutions online or with AI. Then I'll compare and possibly change my solution to be more clean and elegant. I am generally extremely concerned about having the "best" solution to every problem, and I feel great regret in seeing a better solution even if I did manage to solve a problem. There is also some great satisfaction in really digging into the core reason why something is true and exposing it fully in the most direct and efficient way.
  5. Finally, I will sometimes explore uncovered connections to higher math topics. The problems in the MIT sheets are very nice in the sense that there are many such connections, especially in categories such as linear algebra. Finding and exploring them allows one to get more out of each problem.

If you are interested, here is a sample of my solution (sketches) that I decided to TeX up on the linear algebra category. If you want to discuss any problems on the MIT sheets feel free to email me, of course, there is a chance I won't have done it, in particular if it's on the more analytic side or very bashy.

I must say doing these problems helped me tremendously, and I would recommend them to everyone who is taking the Putnam competition seriously. In all honestly, there is no way to get good at math competitions except doing a ton of problems. Of course, there are a lot of problems on the sheets, some of which are P5-P6 level, so it goes without saying solving any significant amount them is a massive endeavor. If you don't have much time, doing all the hearted problems is a good middle ground. They tend to be the type of problems that really teach you something when you solve it.

entry.title: My Opinion on Rust
entry.content:
I attempted to learn Rust, which some hail as a C replacement. Overall, Rust is a fantastic programming language, with lots of great design choices. It is very good at certain tasks, but I can't quite view it as a C replacement.

Pros

Rust makes a lot of good decisions which I think other languages should learn from. The borrow checker is a novel and brilliant idea. Furthermore, the syntax is modernized (I love the type names) and extremely logical (the idea of every scope returning a value is brilliant). Don't even get me started on cargo, it is probably the best build system/package manager I have ever used.

The biggest plus is obviously the novel combination of memory safety and speed. These factors make Rust the best language (in my opinion) for use cases which demand extreme performance and reliability, without requiring too many complicated data structures.

It is clear that Rust is a language in which you declare a lot of intent to the compiler. This can sometimes be a con, as I talk about below. However perhaps it may also become a pro. My hope is that eventually Rust code will be optimized more aggressively than C. For instance, in C, very few are willing to go around putting the restrict keyword everywhere they can. Rust on the other hand sort of forces you to tell the compiler these things, and therefore may allow for more aggressive optimization once compilers adapt to Rust. This is all just speculation through.

Cons

At this point I would like to challenge the reader to implement a doubly linked list or a binary tree in Rust without looking at a guide. This is an intuitive task in C, just draw something on a blackboard and set up all the pointers how you would expect. In Rust it is a pain, there is no way around it. I might have a skill issue, but I find the experience of coding in Rust to be similar to coding in C, except you have an imp on your shoulder (the borrow checker) who won't let you run your code until you convince them that it will work. Rust has bunch of different kinds of objects (Box, Rc, Cell, etc), it turns out they are all pointers but you are only allowed to use each one in a very specific way.

Personally, I would sometimes rather that my compiler just trusted me and ran the code without me needing to convince it that I know what I'm doing. This inevitably leads to memory leaks, segmentation faults, and data corruption, however I can catch this stuff quite well with valgrind. Furthermore, I am a big fan of simplicity, and having a single framework (pointers) which can be extended to accomplish any task is very nice on a moral level. The excessive number of different pointer types Rust has on the other hand is not aesthetically pleasing. However I can understand why it is necessary and I still find Rust to be a fantastic language. I can't wait to see where it goes.
